title: Learning Tools Interoperability (LTI) and auth-provider branching
hook: Learning Tools Interoperability (LTI) 1.3, an OpenID Connect (OIDC) bearer token, and a legacy API key are three shapes of one inbound credential. Pattern matching branches on shape instead of a stringly-typed if pile.

blocks.text: Production auth often receives tokens from multiple providers — LTI launches from a learning management system, OIDC bearer tokens from an identity provider, and legacy API keys from older integrations. Instead of scattering if checks on string fields across controllers, model each provider as a record with the fields it actually needs, then switch on shape with property and list patterns. Keep HTTP framework code out of the decision method so you can unit test with plain records.

entries.plainDefinition: A standard for launching learning tools from a learning management system with signed claims about the user and course context.
entries.example: An LTI 1.3 launch includes an issuer URL and deployment identifier.

entries.plainDefinition: An identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that issues bearer tokens with claims like subject and expiry.
entries.example: A Bearer scheme token with a future ExpiresAt claim is typical OIDC usage.

entries.plainDefinition: An extra boolean condition on a switch arm, evaluated only after the pattern matches.
entries.example: case { Scheme: "Bearer" } t when t.ExpiresAt > utc: runs only for unexpired bearers.

blocks.text: Interviews that mention LTI want to hear that you treat providers as a closed set of data shapes, not as a boolean isLti next to a nullable JSON Web Token (JWT). A switch expression returns a normalized AuthDecision per provider. Unknown or expired tokens should throw or return failure — never silently default to an admin role. That default-to-privileged-path bug is a common security interview trap.

blocks.title: Normalize before you switch
blocks.body: Wire formats send Version = "1.3.0" while your constant pattern expects "1.3". Normalize strings in a preprocessing step, or use a when guard with StartsWith — brittle exact matches miss real LMS payloads.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Parse wire input into a record
items.body: Map headers and claims into InboundToken with Scheme, Version, Issuer, ExpiresAt, and provider-specific fields.

items.title: Switch on property patterns
items.body: Each arm matches the combination of fields that identifies a provider — LTI needs issuer, Bearer needs future expiry.

items.title: Return a normalized decision
items.body: Arms produce AuthDecision with provider id, subject, and roles — no side effects inside the switch.

items.title: Extend with with for snapshots
items.body: Copy the decision with extra roles for instructor launches: decision with { Roles = [.. decision.Roles, "proctor"] }.

diagram.title: Inbound token to auth decision
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  A[InboundToken record] --> B{switch expression}
  B -->|LTI 1.3 + issuer| C[AuthDecision lti13]
  B -->|Bearer + future exp| D[AuthDecision oidc]
  B -->|ApiKey prefix| E[AuthDecision api-key]
  B -->|Bearer expired| F[throw]
  B -->|unknown| G[throw]
  C --> H[optional with for extra roles]

snippet.label: Property patterns on an inbound token
snippet.explanation: LTI requires a non-empty issuer. Bearer requires a future ExpiresAt via when. ApiKey matches a known prefix. A bare Bearer arm catches expired tokens. The discard throws on unknown schemes — no default admin path.

snippet.label: when guard for LTI version prefixes
snippet.explanation: Constant "1.3" misses patch versions like "1.3.0". The is expression binds version, then a boolean guard checks the prefix. Keep switch arms thin by delegating fuzzy checks to helpers.

snippet.label: List pattern on LTI custom claims
snippet.explanation: List patterns validate claim array shape. [var contextId, ..] requires at least one element and binds the first. Empty array and whitespace context id are explicit failure paths.

blocks.text: TypeScript discriminated unions narrow on a kind field: type Token = { kind: 'lti'; issuer: string } | { kind: 'bearer'; exp: number }. C# property patterns can match several fields without a single tag, though a record with an explicit Scheme discriminator is the clearest design. Both approaches beat a chain of if (token.isLti) checks scattered across the codebase.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Matching Scheme strings with different casing from the wire — normalize to a canonical case first. A discard arm that authenticates as guest. Mutating Roles on a shared AuthDecision across concurrent requests — copy with with instead. Matching Version: "1.3" when the LMS sends "1.3.0".

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: model auth providers as discriminated records with an explicit Scheme tag — the same design as TypeScript discriminated unions. Integration tests should deserialize every LMS payload shape (LTI 1.3, OIDC bearer, API key) and assert the switch returns the expected AuthDecision; feed an unknown Scheme and assert 401, not guest access. Log the unmatched token shape in the discard arm for security audits without leaking secrets.

snippet.label: Discriminated union records — TypeScript analogue in C#
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–4: closed hierarchy like TS union on kind. Line 7: positional + property patterns narrow like discriminated union narrowing. Line 11: discard throws — never silent guest.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Erased at runtime — C# keeps types

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: A _ arm that grants guest or admin access on unknown tokens. Matching Scheme strings without normalizing casing from the wire. Mutating Roles on a shared AuthDecision across concurrent requests instead of with snapshot. Saying C# has no equivalent to TypeScript discriminated unions — record hierarchies plus switch are the pattern.

interviewTakeaways: Model auth providers as discriminated records (LTI, OIDC, API key) — switch on shape like TypeScript union narrowing.
Unknown or expired tokens throw or return failed decision — never a privileged discard default.
In production, integration tests per wire shape plus one garbage payload prove the discard arm rejects.
60s: Record hierarchy = discriminated union. Switch expression narrows. when for version prefixes. with snapshots decisions. Discard throws on unknown.
Follow-up: how do property patterns differ from matching a single Kind discriminator field?
commonPitfalls: A _ arm that authenticates as guest gets you rejected — unknown token must fail closed.
Matching Scheme strings with different casing from the wire without normalization.
Strong answer: 'Sealed record per provider. Switch narrows like TS union. Discard throws Unauthorized. with for immutable role updates under concurrency.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: type Token = { kind: 'lti'; issuer: string } | { kind: 'bearer'; exp: number }. TypeScript narrows on kind. C# sealed record hierarchy + switch expression is the runtime-preserved equivalent — types survive after compile.

jsTsCorrelations.concept: Tagged union with switch on shape
jsTsCorrelations.note: JS uses if (token.kind === 'lti') chains without compile-time exhaustiveness. C# switch on record types gives CS8509 when you add a provider and forget an arm — critical for auth code paths.
